cs.u01.title: Lamps on the tower
cs.u01.description: The signal tower shows numbers with a row of lamps. Read them, and set them, in binary.
cs.u01.learnTitle: Every number can be written with just 0 and 1
cs.u01.learn:
In binary each place is worth twice the place to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on. 1101 means one 8, one 4, no 2 and one 1, which is 13.

A computer stores every number this way, as a row of bits, each one on or off.
cs.u01.detail:
To read binary from the left, start at 0 and, for each bit, double what you have and add the bit.

To write a number in binary, take n % 2 for the last bit, then n // 2, and repeat until nothing is left. Python can do both with bin() and int(text, 2), but working it out by hand is what this lesson is about.
cs.u01.example:
# The tower shows numbers with lamps: on is 1, off is 0
lamps = "1101"
value = 0
for lamp in lamps:
    value = value * 2 + int(lamp)
print(value)
print(bin(13))
print(int("1101", 2))
cs.u01.exampleNote: Reading 1101 from the left: 0 doubled plus 1 is 1, then 3, then 6, then 13. bin() writes 13 with a 0b in front to say it is binary, and int(..., 2) reads binary text back.
cs.u01.question: What is the binary 10010 as an ordinary number?
cs.u01.guided: Predict, then run: change the lamps to "11111111" and work out the value first. Then print bin(255) and compare.
cs.u01.challenge:
Write two functions that turn numbers into binary and back.

1. to_binary(n) returns the binary of a whole number n (0 or more) as text, like "1101" for 13 and "0" for 0, without a 0b in front.
2. from_binary(bits) takes text such as "1101" and returns the number, 13.

Try it with // and % before reaching for bin(). Do not ask for input: the check calls your functions with its own values.
hints: For to_binary(), the last bit is n % 2. Then n // 2 shifts everything one place right. Repeat while n is more than 0, putting each new bit in front of the ones you have.
For from_binary(), go through the text from the left: double the value so far, then add the bit, int(bit). 0 needs its own answer in to_binary(), because the loop never runs for it.
With other names, for base 3: digits = str(k % 3) + digits, then k = k // 3, inside a while loop.

errorHints.text: Use the parameter names from each def line, spelled the same way.
Text and numbers do not mix: str() turns a bit into text to join, and int() turns a "1" into the number 1.
to_binary(13) should return "1101": 13 % 2 is 1, then 6 % 2 is 0, then 3 % 2 is 1, then 1 % 2 is 1, read from last to first.
to_binary(0) should return "0": the loop never runs for 0, so give it its own answer.
from_binary("1101") should return 13: double, then add the bit, from the left.
Check a bigger number.
Check text that starts with 0s: they add nothing.

similarExample.code:
def to_base3(k):
    digits = ""
    while k > 0:
        digits = str(k % 3) + digits
        k = k // 3
    return digits

print(to_base3(10))
similarExample.note: The same idea in base 3, where each place is worth three times the one to its right. Your lamps use base 2, and 0 needs care.

otherWays.note: Python's own tools: bin() gives "0b1101", and [2:] cuts off the 0b. Now you know what they do inside.
to_binary() calling itself on a smaller number, which the recursion unit explains, and from_binary() adding up the place values from the right.

cs.u01.title: Colours on the flags
cs.u01.description: The tower signals with coloured flags, written as six hex digits. Turn them into amounts of red, green and blue, and back.
cs.u01.learnTitle: Sixteen digits, and why colours use them
cs.u01.learn: Hexadecimal, or hex, has sixteen digits: 0 to 9, then a to f for ten to fifteen. Each place is worth sixteen times the one to its right, so ff is 15 × 16 + 15, which is 255.
cs.u01.detail:
One hex digit is exactly four bits, so two of them hold a byte, any number from 0 to 255.

That is why screen colours are written #ff8800: two hex digits each for red, green and blue. int(text, 16) reads hex, and f"{n:02x}" writes a number as two hex digits.
cs.u01.example:
# A flag colour: red, green and blue, each from 0 to 255
red = 255
green = 136
blue = 0
print(hex(green))
print(f"#{red:02x}{green:02x}{blue:02x}")
print(int("88", 16))
cs.u01.exampleNote: 136 is eight 16s and eight 1s, so it is 88 in hex. :02x writes each amount as two hex digits, and int("88", 16) reads them back.
cs.u01.question: What colour is #00ff00?
cs.u01.why: No red, the most green (ff is 255), and no blue.
cs.u01.guided: Predict, then run: make the flag purple, with lots of red and blue and no green, and print its code. Then try 300 for red and see what happens to the code.
cs.u01.starter: # Define hex_to_rgb(colour) and rgb_to_hex(red, green, blue)
cs.u01.challenge:
Write two functions that turn colour codes into amounts and back.

1. hex_to_rgb(colour) takes a colour such as "#ff8800" (capitals allowed) and returns a list of its red, green and blue amounts, [255, 136, 0].
2. rgb_to_hex(red, green, blue) returns the colour code, always with # and six lowercase hex digits, such as "#0a0b0c".

Do not ask for input: the check calls your functions with its own values.
hints: Each amount is two hex digits. Their value is the first digit times 16, plus the second. The text "0123456789abcdef".index(d) turns a digit into its value.
For rgb_to_hex(), the two digits of an amount are value // 16 and value % 16, looked up the other way. Small amounts still need two digits: 10 is 0a.
With other names: high, low = divmod(n, 16) splits a byte, and int("c8", 16) reads one back.

errorHints.text: Use the parameter names from each def line, spelled the same way.
A digit was not found. Make the text lowercase and take off the # before reading the digits.
Check what each function takes: hex_to_rgb() takes one piece of text, and rgb_to_hex() three numbers.
hex_to_rgb("#ff8800") should return [255, 136, 0].
rgb_to_hex(10, 11, 12) should return "#0a0b0c": every amount gets two digits, even a small one.
hex_to_rgb("#00FF7f") has capitals: make the text lowercase first, or read both kinds.
Check the largest amounts.
Check the smallest amounts.

similarExample.code:
def split_byte(n):
    high, low = divmod(n, 16)
    return high, low

print(split_byte(200))
print(int("c8", 16))
similarExample.note: A byte split into its two hex digits, and read back. Your colours have three bytes each.

otherWays.note: int(..., 16) and the :02x format do the conversions; slicing picks out each pair of digits.
The whole colour as one number: red is worth 256 × 256, green 256, and blue 1.

cs.u01.title: Coded messages
cs.u01.concept: Text · characters as numbers, and bytes
cs.u01.description: Messages leave the tower as numbers. Shift letters to make a simple code, and count the bytes a message really takes.
cs.u01.learn: A computer stores each character as a number called its code point: ord("a") is 97 and chr(97) is "a". The letters a to z have codes one after another, so moving a letter along the alphabet is adding to its code.
cs.u01.detail:
To send text, its code points are written as bytes using an encoding.

UTF-8, the most common one, uses one byte for each plain English letter and more for others: é takes two bytes and many emoji four. So len(text) counts characters, while len(text.encode("utf-8")) counts bytes.
cs.u01.example:
# Every character is stored as a number
print(ord("A"), ord("a"))
print(chr(98))
print(len("café"))
print(len("café".encode("utf-8")))
cs.u01.exampleNote: Capital A and small a have different codes. "café" has four characters but five bytes, because é takes two in UTF-8.
cs.u01.question: What does chr(ord("y") + 2) give?
cs.u01.why: y is 121, and 123 is the character {. To wrap around to a, the code has to come back to the start of the alphabet, which % 26 does.
cs.u01.guided: Predict, then run: print ord("z") and chr(ord("z") + 1). Then measure len("🙂".encode("utf-8")).
cs.u01.challenge:
Write two functions about text.

1. shift(message, steps) moves every small letter a to z that many places along the alphabet, wrapping round from z to a, and leaves every other character as it is: shift("abc xyz", 2) returns "cde zab". steps can be negative or bigger than 26.
2. byte_count(text) returns how many bytes text takes in UTF-8.

Do not ask for input: the check calls your functions with its own values.
hints: For each character, check whether it is a small letter. If it is, work out its place in the alphabet, 0 for a to 25 for z, with ord(ch) - ord("a").
Add steps to the place, and % 26 keeps it from 0 to 25, even for negative steps. chr() of the place plus ord("a") gives the new letter. encode("utf-8") turns text into bytes for byte_count().
With other names, for digits: chr((ord(d) - ord("0") + 1) % 10 + ord("0")) moves a digit one along, wrapping 9 round to 0.

errorHints.text: Use the parameter names from each def line, spelled the same way.
ord() takes one character and chr() one number. Build the new message by joining characters.
shift("abc xyz", 2) should return "cde zab": z wraps round to b, and the space stays a space.
shift("hello", -1) should return "gdkkn": negative steps go back along the alphabet.
byte_count("café") should return 5: é takes two bytes in UTF-8.
Check a shift bigger than 26: it wraps round more than once.
Check capital letters, digits and marks: they stay as they are.

similarExample.note: Digits moved along their own ten codes, wrapping round. Your shift moves letters along twenty-six.

otherWays.note: translate() swaps every letter at once, using a table from the alphabet to the shifted alphabet.
The same steps in one line with join(); encode() uses UTF-8 when no encoding is named.

cs.u01.title: The ledger that would not balance
cs.u01.description: The tower ledger adds up prices. Find out why decimals drift, and keep money exact by counting cents.
cs.u01.learnTitle: Some decimals cannot be stored exactly
cs.u01.learn:
A float stores a number in binary, like a fraction with a power of two underneath. 0.5 is ½, so it is exact, but 0.1 needs a pattern of bits that goes on for ever, so Python keeps the closest float it can.

Add two of these tiny errors and they show: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004.
cs.u01.detail: Whole numbers in Python are always exact. So money is usually counted in whole cents, and turned into dollars only for showing. Never compare floats with ==; round them, or use math.isclose(), which unit 7 met.
cs.u01.example:
# Decimals are stored in binary, and most are not exact
print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(round(0.1 + 0.2, 2))
cents = 10 + 20
print(cents / 100)
cs.u01.exampleNote: The tiny error makes == say False. Rounding hides it for showing; counting in whole cents avoids it altogether.
cs.u01.question: Which of these is stored exactly as a float?
cs.u01.why: 0.5 is one half, a power of two. 0.1 and 0.3 need bits that never end.
cs.u01.guided: Predict, then run: add 0.1 ten times in a loop and print the total. Then do the same with 10 cents, and divide by 100 at the end.
cs.u01.challenge:
Prices arrive as text such as "4.35", "12" or "0.5" (which means 50 cents). Add them up without float().

1. Write to_cents(price), which returns the whole number of cents: 435, 1200 or 50.
2. Write add_prices(prices), which takes a list of such prices and returns the total as text with exactly two decimal places, such as "0.30".

Do not ask for input: the check calls your functions with its own values.
hints: Split the text at the point: the part before it is dollars, the part after it is cents, but "5" after the point means 50 cents, not 5.
Pad the cents part to two digits on the right before turning it into a number. add_prices() adds up cents, then splits the total into dollars and cents with // and %.
With other names: minutes, _, seconds = "3:07".partition(":") splits a time, and f"{n:02d}" always writes two digits.

errorHints.text: Use the parameter names from each def line, spelled the same way.
int() could not read part of a price. A price without a point, such as "12", has no cents part: treat it as 0 cents.
add_prices() returns text: build it with an f-string, or str(), from the dollars and the cents.
to_cents("4.35") should return 435. If you got 434, float() crept in: 4.35 × 100 is stored as 434.99999999999994.
to_cents("0.5") should return 50: one digit after the point means tens of cents.
add_prices(["0.10", "0.20"]) should return "0.30", exactly, with two digits after the point.
Check a price with no point at all.
Check a longer list of prices.

similarExample.note: A time split at its colon and counted in whole seconds. Your prices split at the point, and the cents can have one digit or two.

otherWays.note: ljust() pads the cents on the right; divmod() gives dollars and cents together.
rjust() pads the cents on the left, so 5 cents shows as 05. Python also has a decimal module for exact decimals, used by real money code, but not available on this page.

cs.u03.title: Search the shelf
cs.u03.concept: Searching · one item at a time
cs.u03.description: The archive keeps records on long shelves. Search them one by one, and count how many you had to look at.
cs.u03.learnTitle: Look at each item until you find it
cs.u03.learn: A linear search checks the items in order, from the first, until it finds the one it wants or runs out. It works on any list, sorted or not.
cs.u03.detail: Counting how many items it looks at, its steps, tells you how much work it did. Found at the start: 1 step. Found at the end, or not there at all: as many steps as there are items. Doubling the list doubles the worst case.
cs.u03.example:
# Look along the shelf, one box at a time
shelf = ["rope", "map", "lamp", "key"]
looks = 0
found_at = -1
for i in range(len(shelf)):
    looks = looks + 1
    if shelf[i] == "lamp":
        found_at = i
        break
print(found_at, looks)
cs.u03.exampleNote: lamp is at position 2, and finding it took 3 looks: rope, map, lamp. break stops the loop as soon as it is found.
cs.u03.question: If the shelf held 1,000 boxes and the one wanted was not there, how many looks would it take?
cs.u03.why: To be sure something is missing, a linear search has to look at every item.
cs.u03.guided: Predict, then run: search for "key", then for "sword", which is not there, and compare the counts.
cs.u03.challenge:
Write find(items, target), which looks through the list items from the start.

1. Return a list of two numbers: the position of the first item equal to target, and how many items it looked at to get there.
2. If target is not there, return -1 and the number of items it looked at, which is all of them.

Do not ask for input: the check calls your functions with its own values.
hints: Keep a count of looks that starts at 0, and go through the positions in order, adding one each time you look at an item.
As soon as an item matches, return its position and the count, together. If the loop ends, nothing matched: return -1 and the count after the loop.
With other names: for spot in range(len(row)): with tries = tries + 1 inside, and return [spot, tries] when row[spot] == wanted.

errorHints.text: Use the parameter names from the def line, spelled the same way.
A position is past the end: range(len(items)) gives exactly the positions there are.
find(["rope", "map", "lamp", "key"], "lamp") should return [2, 3]: position 2, after looking at 3 items.
When target is not there, return -1 and the number of items looked at: all of them.
Check a list where the target is the first item: one look.
Check a list with the target in it twice: the first one counts.
Check an empty list.

similarExample.note: A linear search for the first even number, counting looks. Yours returns a position, not the item.

otherWays.note: enumerate() numbers the items as it goes, here from 1, so the count and the position come together.
A while loop that stops at a match or at the end. The number of looks follows from where it stopped.

cs.u03.title: Halve the shelf
cs.u03.concept: Searching · binary search on a sorted list
cs.u03.description: When the archive is sorted, you can skip half of it with every look. Find records in a handful of steps.
cs.u03.learnTitle: Throw away half with every look
cs.u03.learn:
In a sorted list, look at the middle item. If it is the one you want, you are done.

If it is too small, what you want can only be to its right; too big, only to its left. Either way, half the list is gone after one look.
cs.u03.detail:
Keep two positions, low and high, for the part still worth searching, and look at middle = (low + high) // 2.

Stop when they cross. A thousand items take at most ten looks, a million about twenty. It only works if the list is sorted.
cs.u03.exampleNote: 21 is too small, so the left half goes; then 42 is found on the second look. A linear search would have needed six.
cs.u03.question: About how many looks does a binary search need for a sorted list of 1,000 items, at most?
cs.u03.why: Halving 1,000 ten times gets below one: 500, 250, 125, 63, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
cs.u03.guided: Predict, then run: search for 3, the first item, and for 50, which is not there, and count the looks each time.
cs.u03.challenge:
Write binary_find(items, target) for a list items sorted from smallest to largest.

1. Search it as the lesson does: keep low and high, look at middle = (low + high) // 2 each time, and move low or high past it.
2. Return a list: the position of target and how many middles you looked at.
3. If target is not there, return -1 and the number of looks.

Do not ask for input: the check calls your functions with its own values.
hints: Start with low at the first position and high at the last. Keep going while low is no more than high, and count one look each time round.
If the middle item is smaller than target, the target can only be to its right: low becomes middle + 1. If it is bigger, high becomes middle - 1. Without the + 1 and - 1 the loop can get stuck.
With other names, guessing a number from 1 to 100: mid = (lo + hi) // 2, then lo = mid + 1 when the secret is bigger.

errorHints.text: Use the parameter names from the def line, spelled the same way.
binary_find([3, 8, 15, 21, 30, 42, 57], 42) should return [5, 2]: 21 first, then 42.
When target is not there, low and high cross; return -1 and the number of looks.
binary_find([3, 8, 15, 21, 30, 42, 57], 3) should return [0, 3]: 21, then 8, then 3.
Check a long list: the looks should stay few.
Check a list with one item.

similarExample.note: Guessing a number from 1 to 100 by halving, which is a binary search over the numbers themselves. Yours searches a list and returns a position.

otherWays.note: Moving low or high in one line, with a conditional expression.
The search calling itself on the half that is left, a recursive binary search.

cs.u03.title: How the work grows
cs.u03.concept: Searching · counting steps as lists grow
cs.u03.description: Compare the two searches by counting, not timing: how many looks does each need as the archive grows?
cs.u03.learnTitle: Count the steps, not the seconds
cs.u03.learn:
How long a program takes depends on the computer, so computer scientists count steps instead.

The question is how the steps grow as the input grows: a linear search of n items needs up to n looks, a binary search only as many as the times n can be halved.
cs.u03.detail: Halving: 8 items halve to 4, 2, 1, 0, which is four halvings, so a binary search of 8 needs at most 4 looks. Doubling the list adds only one more look. That gap is why sorted data is worth the effort of sorting.
cs.u03.example:
# How many halvings until nothing is left?
for size in [1, 2, 7, 8, 1000]:
    n = size
    halvings = 0
    while n > 0:
        n = n // 2
        halvings = halvings + 1
    print(size, halvings)
cs.u03.exampleNote: 1,000 items need only 10 halvings. Going from 7 items to 8 adds one, because 8 is a power of two.
cs.u03.question: A list grows from 1,000 items to 2,000. How many more looks can a binary search need, at most?
cs.u03.why: Doubling the list adds one halving.
cs.u03.guided: Predict, then run: add 1,000,000 to the sizes and guess its halvings first. Then add a column with the linear worst case, the size itself.
cs.u03.challenge:
Write three functions that count the looks a search needs.

1. linear_worst(n) returns the most looks a linear search needs for a list of n items.
2. binary_worst(n) returns the most looks a binary search needs, which is how many times n can be halved with // 2 before it reaches 0 (0 for an empty list).
3. compare(sizes) takes a list of sizes and returns a list of [size, linear, binary] lists, one per size, in the same order.

Do not ask for input: the check calls your functions with its own values.
hints: The linear worst case is simply every item. For the binary one, count halvings in a loop: n = n // 2, adding one each time, while n is more than 0.
compare() builds a list: for each size, a list of the size and the two counts, worked out by calling the other two functions.
With other names: doublings = 0, then while value < limit: value = value * 2 and doublings = doublings + 1.

errorHints.text: Use the parameter names from each def line, and call the other functions by their names.
compare() returns a list of lists: append [size, linear, binary] for each size.
binary_worst(8) should return 4: 8, 4, 2, 1, then 0.
binary_worst(0) should return 0: an empty list needs no looks.
Check a very big size.
Check an odd size just below a power of two.

similarExample.code:
value = 1
doublings = 0
while value < 1000:
    value = value * 2
    doublings = doublings + 1
print(doublings)
similarExample.note: Counting doublings up to 1,000 rather than halvings down from it. The two counts match, which is the heart of binary search.

otherWays.note: bit_length() is how many bits n needs in binary, which is exactly how many times it can be halved. Unit 1 and unit 3 meet.
log2() counts halvings with a formula. It is the "log n" you will meet in books about algorithms.
